function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

The user asks: "I am planning a trip to New York City... what will be the temperature next week there?" They want forecast for NYC next week. We need to use the Open-Meteo API via the provided function. We need to call the function with appropriate parameters: latitude and longitude for NYC. Latitude ~40.7128 N, longitude -74.0060 W. Use the function requests_get. Provide URL: "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast". Provide params: latitude=40.7128, longitude=-74.0060, maybe also daily=temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min? But we can just ask for daily temperature. Let's check Open-Meteo docs: For daily forecasts, you can specify daily=temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min. Also need start_date and end_date. Next week: starting tomorrow? Or next 7 days? Let's assume next 7 days from today. Today is unknown but we can compute relative dates. But we can't compute dynamic date here. We can approximate: start_date=YYYY-MM-DD. But we don't know current date. We could ask for next 7 days from now. But we can provide placeholder like "start_date=2026-11-15", "end_date=2026-11-21". But we don't know actual date. We can ask for next 7 days from now. But we can just call the function with start_date and end_date as placeholders. But the function expects specific values. We might not have to provide them if we want all available forecast. But we can provide daily=temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min. The function returns JSON.

We need to call the function. Then respond with the result. So we call the function with:

{
"url": "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast",
"params": {
"latitude": 40.7128,
"longitude": -74.0060,
"daily": ["temperature_2m_max","temperature_2m_min"],
"start_date": "2026-11-15",
"end_date": "2026-11-21"
}
}

But we don't know today's date. We can approximate. But we can ask for next week from now. But we can just provide the function call with start_date and end_date as placeholders. But the function may return error if dates invalid. But we can still call. Let's call with start_date=2026-11-15, end_date=2026-11-21. That covers next week. We'll then parse the returned JSON. Then answer accordingly.
